method: Flesch Kincaid grade plus 5 estimates. Punctuated sentences and standalone task lines are sentence units. Fixed syllable overrides and vowel-group heuristic inherited from the reference method. Text and SHA-256 are retained per corpus. Estimates are not a learner assessment. Staff text, titles, codes and dates excluded. Fragmentary log prompts have limited numerical validity. Artist names and vocabulary are taught aloud. No executable is supplied.

Choose Matisse's movable shapes or Thomas's repeated marks from two spoken descriptions. Use an adult's model for the first repeat, then choose your own change. Say, point or dictate: 'I chose ... because ...'.
Identify a detail from each artist card. Make two short trials in your chosen form, then choose one feature for your own first response and explain why.
Try the same idea in two forms. You could use marks, then gestures. Choose one form. Say why it fits your idea. The next level task is optional.

Henri Matisse made paintings and later developed cut-outs as artworks in their own right. Assistants painted paper. He cut shapes and directed their arrangement. The shapes could move while he tested an idea. This gives us a way to discuss changing a method and revising a design.
Alma Thomas developed an abstract painting style using repeated coloured marks. Nature and space helped her find ideas. In The Eclipse, made in 1970, a dark blue centre sits within rings of colour. The centre is off to one side. This arrangement can suggest a moment of movement and change.

Use both artist cards. Note one fact about each artist. Say which method interests you. Give your reason. Set one skill to practise. You can draw, speak or write.
Keep both facts, your view and reason, and your skill goal. Say which card you used. An adult can write your words.

Recall your first response. You may keep the art form or change your method.
Recall one detail about Matisse and one about Thomas. Listen to the cards again if needed.
Watch one change to the original seed example. What changed? Why?
Try two versions of one feature. Ask what your partner notices.
Hinge: must you use feedback, ignore it, or consider it and choose for your purpose?
Develop your own response. Test one change. Choose the version to keep.
Use a quiet or silent route if you prefer. You may pause or ask for help.
Explain the artist link and your own choices. Record your change and its effect in the arts log.
Choose one next step. Keep your response and log evidence together.
